Q1 2022 Objection Handling Refresh: Recall Context
Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 11, 2022
Distribution: Reconstructive sales team (internal use only — do not forward externally)

Purpose
As we prep the field for potential questions ahead of any customer-facing communications on the cup lot matter, I want to make sure everyone is drawing a clean line between two separate topics. We've seen some blending of these in call notes and I want to nip that before it becomes a pattern.

Two distinct issues — keep them separate

1. Coating/lot issue (Cork manufacturing) — a limited number of acetabular cup lots (V-2200 through V-2299, produced Nov 2021–Feb 2022) showed a coating adhesion irregularity identified during incoming inspection at two facilities. This is a manufacturing quality matter tied to a specific production window. Quality and Regulatory are running lot traceability now; more to follow from Dana's team on timing/scope.

2. Bearing surface / revision rate discussion — this is the ongoing, industry-wide conversation around metal-on-metal wear performance and registry data (NJR, AJRR) that surgeons have been raising since last fall. That's a separate clinical topic and is already addressed in the FAQ Priya's and Dana's teams sent out in September, along with the Dear Doctor letter and label update language.

Suggested script if asked
"This is a manufacturing quality issue with a specific batch, separate from the industry-wide bearing surface discussion. We identified it through our own inspection process and are addressing it directly with affected accounts. It's not related to the wear performance questions you may have seen in the registry data — that's a separate topic we've already given you materials on."

Do
- Refer back to the September FAQ for revision-rate/registry questions.
- Keep coating questions focused on lot numbers, not wear mechanism.
- Loop in your RSM if a surgeon pushes on both topics at once.

Don't
- Speculate on root cause beyond "manufacturing process deviation under review."
- Use the words "recall" or "withdrawal" until we have official notice language — more on that soon.

Questions to me or Jenna. Thanks for staying disciplined on this — it matters.

Subject: RE: wear test re-run results - concerning

Dana, looping you in per Tom's note below - wanted your read on this before we decide how to route it.

Tom re-ran wear testing at 55 degrees inclination (outside the standard 45-degree ISO 14242 protocol used for the original design verification) and is seeing 4-6x higher wear rates across all three cup sizes tested. This wasn't part of the original DV protocol, so per procedure it isn't captured anywhere in the DHF as a known failure mode - it's new data from an internal exploratory test.

My question is whether this needs to be reported to FDA as new information given the AI request we just closed out on MDR trending, or whether this is still design-engineering-internal at this stage - i.e., something we track and evaluate before it rises to a reportability question. I don't want to under-call this, but I also don't want to characterize an off-protocol bench test as a confirmed safety signal prematurely.

Dana, can you weigh in on whether 803.50/803.53 considerations apply here, or if this stays with Tom's team for now while we assess correlation with the complaint clusters? Would like to align before this goes further.

Priya

Priya, Carlos,

Finished the re-run I mentioned a few weeks back. Wanted to test the cup at 55 degrees inclination instead of the standard 45 we used for the original 14242 protocol, just to see what happens outside the "ideal" implant orientation, since we know a chunk of surgeons run steeper than textbook.

Results aren't good. Wear rates at 55 deg are running 4-6x what we see at 45 deg, consistently across the three cup sizes I tested. Attached is the raw data and summary charts - Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx. Take a look at the tab labeled "edge loading summary," that's where it's most obvious.

This is bugging me because if surgeons are landing cups anywhere near 55 deg in practice, we'd expect elevated metal release from edge loading, and that lines up uncomfortably well with the complaint clusters we've seen out of Atlanta and Nashville - the cobalt/chromium numbers on a few of those patients were high enough that people noticed. I'm not saying that's definitely what's happening, but it's not nothing either.

Priya - given FDA is already asking us about MDR trending, does this need to go up to regulatory? Feels like something Dana should at least know about before it comes up on its own. Carlos, flagging you too since this could affect how we're positioning cup size/inclination guidance to reps and surgeons.

Let me know how you want to handle it.

Tom

Re: Concerns regarding ApexHip metal ion levels in my patients

Dear Priya:

I am writing to request that Veridian review a concerning cluster of three ApexHip patients in my practice. All have presented with persistent groin pain and, in two cases, swelling and reduced function that is not readily explained by radiographic findings alone.

Serum testing has shown elevated cobalt levels in each patient, ranging from 18 to 25 ppb. Chromium is also elevated, although less consistently. The patients were implanted at different times over the past year, and I am in the process of completing additional imaging and workup. At present, I do not believe infection is the likely explanation.

The cup lot numbers available from our records are V-2039, V-2041, and V-2044. Please determine whether Quality has identified any complaint, manufacturing, or device-history concerns associated with those lots, or whether similar metal-ion reports have been received elsewhere. I recognize that three cases do not establish causation, but the similarity of the clinical presentation warrants a prompt look.

I would also ask that the review not be limited to lot history. If there is a broader design, bearing, positioning, or wear-related issue that could be contributing to elevated ion levels, I would like to understand what data Veridian has and what follow-up it intends to undertake.

One patient is likely to require revision, and I can make explant components and associated periprosthetic tissue available for analysis if that would be useful. Please advise regarding chain-of-custody requirements and the appropriate contact for specimen handling.

As a design consultant to Veridian and an early supporter of ApexHip, I find this personally concerning. I expect the company to investigate these reports carefully and communicate candidly about what is found.

Sincerely,

Dr. Marcus Feld
Atlanta Joint Institute

From: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer

Subject: Q3 2022 Apex Litigation Reserve — Draft Memo

Attached is the current draft for the Q3 close materials. I am circulating this now because the proposed reserve is material enough that I do not want the first substantive discussion to occur in the audit committee pre-read.

We are proposing an $18.0 million reserve for ApexHip-related claims and associated costs in Q3 2022. The working allocation is as follows:

| Component | Proposed Reserve | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Anticipated product-liability / litigation exposure | $11.0M | Filed and threatened patient claims, counsel assessment, complaint trend, revision signal |
| Recall-related warranty and replacement costs | $7.0M | V-2200–V-2299 field action, replacement product, credits, hospital handling and related service costs |
| Total | $18.0M |  |

The $11.0M litigation component remains an estimate rather than a case-specific accrual schedule. We have a relatively small number of asserted claims today, but the underlying indicators are moving in the wrong direction. In particular, the March 2021 NJR reporting showed a five-year Apex revision rate of 7.1%, compared with a 3.2% class average. The later registry information has not provided a basis to dismiss that signal. TrackWise complaint counts also continue to rise, including complaints involving elevated Co/Cr levels, pain, suspected ARMD, and early revision.

The $7.0M recall component is limited to the June field action for cup lots V-2200 through V-2299. That estimate includes expected replacement and credit exposure for distributed product, hospital administrative costs where contractually required, return processing, and an allowance for additional warranty requests. It does not assume that the coating issue and the metal-ion allegations share a common cause. For accounting purposes, however, both items are Apex-related and need to be visible together in the Q3 discussion.

Hannah: please run the variance cases against the current FY22 forecast and provide (1) the Q3 P&L effect, (2) cash timing through Q4 2023, and (3) the revenue sensitivity if accounts defer Apex purchases following the recall notice. I would also like a base, downside, and severe-case view rather than a single-point estimate.

Rachel: please review the proposed contingency language, especially the distinction between known recall costs and estimated exposure from asserted or anticipated claims. I do not want us to overstate certainty where the claims landscape is still developing, but the committee will reasonably ask why the reserve is increasing now.

Rob: absent a significant change in the underlying numbers, my recommendation is that we book the full $18.0M in Q3 and discuss it with the audit committee as a discrete Apex matter rather than burying it in the broader warranty line.

Please send comments by noon Monday so we can finalize the pre-read package.

Owen

Human Resources — Confidential Manager Check-in Note

Date: August 15, 2022
Prepared by: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
Subject: Mid-Year Check-in - Tom Halvorsen

I met with Tom on August 11 as part of the informal mid-year check-in cycle for the ApexHip engineering group. This was not a formal performance review and no action is required in Workday at this time.

Tom continues to perform strongly in his Senior Design Engineer role. His technical knowledge of the Apex system, including historical design decisions, wear-testing methodology, and supporting DHF documentation, remains unusually deep. His manager reports that he is responsive on technical questions, thorough with data review, and dependable when cross-functional teams need historical context. Tom has also been helpful to newer engineers who are trying to understand the legacy KBT coating work and the relationship between material specifications and product performance.

The main concern coming out of the conversation is engagement and role fit. Tom stated that he is increasingly interested in moving out of the day-to-day Apex work and into a role with more forward-looking development responsibility. He specifically mentioned Advanced Materials as an area he would like to explore, particularly work involving coatings, tribology, and test-method development.

Tom did not characterize this as an immediate resignation risk, but he was candid that he has felt discouraged and “stuck” since the recall announcement. He described the current work as highly reactive and said he is spending more time revisiting prior decisions than doing engineering he considers productive. He was careful not to raise a specific complaint about any individual. His comments were more generally about the volume of follow-up requests, the pace of cross-functional review, and his concern that technical input is sometimes sought after decisions have already been framed.

I recommend that Tom’s manager schedule a focused retention conversation before the end of August. The discussion should acknowledge his contributions, clarify near-term expectations, and ask directly what type of work would make the next 12–18 months sustainable for him. Given his background, a lateral move or partial assignment to Advanced Materials could be a reasonable option by Q4, subject to business need and headcount planning.

I will connect separately with the Advanced Materials HR lead regarding anticipated openings and will keep this note confidential within the appropriate management/HR group.

As agreed by the review team and executive leadership, Veridian will maintain active commercial distribution of ApexHip while implementing an immediate Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling update to address emerging registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
The primary driver for this communication is data presented from the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report, which identified a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, compared to an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% across contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. While internal clinical evaluations indicate that well-positioned constructs continue to demonstrate strong clinical survivorship, registry data and internal engineering assessments correlate early revisions predominantly with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) linked to elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The draft notification emphasizes patient safety, precise surgical technique, and targeted post-operative vigilance:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: We advise clinicians to establish heightened routine clinical and radiographic follow-up protocols for all implanted ApexHip patients, with particular attention to individuals receiving larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic blood metal-ion quantification (whole blood cobalt and chromium) should be considered annually or upon any presentation of unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions strongly correlate with edge-loading phenomena. The revised labeling explicitly instructs surgeons to target an acetabular cup inclination angle within 40° to 45° and anteversion between 15° and 20°. Operating outside these ranges—specifically exceeding 50° of operative abduction—markedly increases the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and premature component loosening.

Attendees: Rob Castellano (CEO), Rachel Steinberg (GC), Owen Park (CFO), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (CMO), Greg Novak (Director, PMS)

1. Purpose
Ms. Steinberg opened the meeting noting that it was convened following formation of MDL 3102 (N.D. Ind., Dec. 2023) and was intended to reassess ApexHip's market status in light of cumulative registry and claims data since the September 2021 Registry Signal Review.

2. Registry and Post-Market Data (Novak)
Mr. Novak presented updated NJR and AJRR figures showing the 5-year revision rate gap versus class average has widened further since the March 2021 report (7.1% at that time). He stated the trend has been consistent and directionally worsening across three consecutive reporting cycles, and that the metal-ion/ARMD signal first identified internally in 2019 (Halvorsen re-analysis) remains the dominant driver of revisions.

3. Clinical Assessment (Dr. Adeyemi)
Dr. Adeyemi stated that his risk-benefit assessment has changed since 2021. He noted that at the time of the Registry Signal Review, the available data supported a labeling-based mitigation given uncertainty about whether the signal would stabilize. He said the additional two-plus years of registry evidence, combined with the volume and pattern of ARMD-related revisions, no longer support that conclusion in his clinical judgment. He recommended the company treat withdrawal as a live option rather than a last resort.

4. Financial Exposure (Park)
Mr. Park reviewed reserve trends since the $18M Q3 2022 booking, noting continued upward pressure from claims volume following MDL formation. He cautioned that reserve estimates carry significant uncertainty pending further claims development but agreed the trajectory is unfavorable.

5. Legal Considerations (Steinberg)
Ms. Steinberg advised that MDL formation changes the litigation posture materially and that the company should evaluate withdrawal on its own merits, separate from the 2021 decision, rather than treating the earlier decision as controlling precedent. She noted potential regulatory notification obligations and litigation implications of a voluntary withdrawal and stated she would prepare an option analysis addressing both.

6. Regulatory Considerations (Okonkwo)
Ms. Okonkwo noted that any withdrawal decision would require coordination with FDA and consideration of MDR obligations, and offered to support Ms. Steinberg's analysis from a regulatory-process standpoint.

7. Discussion
Mr. Castellano stated that the group appeared to be converging on the view that withdrawal warrants serious evaluation, but that no decision should be made without the fuller analysis. He asked that the option analysis be brought back to this group before any recommendation goes further.

8. Action Items
- Ms. Steinberg to prepare a withdrawal option analysis, including regulatory and litigation implications (target: mid-January 2024).
- Mr. Novak to continue tracking incoming registry updates.
- Dr. Adeyemi to draft a written summary of his revised clinical assessment for inclusion in the analysis.

No final decision was made. Meeting adjourned 3:15 PM.
